paragraphs: Regularized least squares fits observations while penalizing undesirable properties of the solution. LASSO, which uses an absolute-value penalty, is a prominent example. This paper studies how such solutions behave as problems become large, when the measurement matrix is random. The central question is whether precise performance predictions depend on the particular distribution used to generate that matrix.

Previous expressions described LASSO performance in several settings, especially matrices with independent Gaussian entries. Experiments had suggested that some non-Gaussian matrices follow the same expressions. The paper supplies a theoretical justification for this observation when the relevant distribution is sub-Gaussian, establishing a qualified form of universality across matrix distributions.

The analysis also extends earlier expressions to a wider family of regularization functions and relaxes conditions on the random matrix. Its contribution is therefore a broader basis for predicting asymptotic statistics, including average quadratic risk. These are large-problem results under specified distributional conditions; universality here does not mean that every matrix distribution or every finite problem has identical performance.
neurips-2017-a-universal-analysis-of-lar.tldr: The paper establishes when large-scale LASSO and other regularized least-squares solutions share asymptotic behavior across different random measurement distributions.

paragraphs: Classification becomes difficult to manage when the possible labels number in the tens of thousands. One approach converts the original task into binary classification over pairs of examples. This changes the form of the learning problem, but can create a very large expanded dataset. Uneven class frequencies add another challenge because many classes have relatively little data.

The paper introduces a double sampling strategy on top of this pair-based reduction. Its goals are to reduce the number of training pairs and address the long-tailed class distributions common in large classification problems. The theoretical result shows that this sampling does not change the consistency of empirical risk minimization for the double sample reduction.

Experiments use the DMOZ and Wikipedia collections with between 10,000 and 100,000 classes. The evaluation considers training time, prediction time, memory use, and predictive performance against state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution connects computational savings with a statistical justification: aggressive pair selection can make the reduction more manageable while preserving the stated consistency property.
neurips-2017-aggressive-sampling-for-mul.tldr: A double sampling strategy makes pair-based classification with many classes more manageable while preserving the reduction’s stated statistical consistency.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much data is needed when several players want to learn the same underlying concept and every player needs an accurate classifier. Learning separately wastes opportunities to share information. However, a collaborative procedure must satisfy all players simultaneously, so its data requirements need to be compared with those of an ordinary single-player task.

The authors formalize this comparison through overhead: the collaborative sample complexity divided by the single-player sample complexity. They develop algorithms for personalized and centralized versions of the problem. With k players, the respective overhead bounds are O(ln(k)) and O(ln²(k)), making the additional data requirement grow slowly with the number of participants.

These bounds give an exponential improvement over the naive approach without information sharing. The paper also proves an Ω(ln(k)) lower bound, establishing that some increasing cost of collaboration is unavoidable in this model. Together, the bounds identify the achievable overhead up to a logarithmic factor and show how sharing information changes the statistical cost of serving many learners.
neurips-2017-collaborative-pac-learning-.tldr: Collaborative learning algorithms achieve logarithmic or squared-logarithmic sample overhead, with a lower bound showing near-tight dependence on the number of players.

paragraphs: Oja’s iteration estimates a leading principal component while data arrive as a stream. It updates a running estimate instead of repeatedly solving the full principal component analysis problem, offering lower time and memory demands. This paper examines how that stochastic update evolves, with the aim of explaining its convergence and the accuracy obtainable from a finite amount of data.

The authors describe the normalized estimate as a Markov chain on the unit sphere: its location is continuous, but updates occur at discrete steps. They then use diffusion approximations and weak convergence tools to characterize the iteration through three phases. This gives a mathematical description of the learning dynamics across different stages.

The three-phase analysis leads to a finite-sample error bound for the running estimate. Under the additional assumption that samples are bounded, this bound matches the minimax information lower bound for PCA. The finding connects a computationally economical streaming procedure with statistically optimal error behavior in the stated setting, while retaining the bounded-sample qualification.
neurips-2017-diffusion-approximations-fo.tldr: A three-phase diffusion analysis of Oja’s streaming PCA update yields an error bound matching the minimax lower bound under bounded samples.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks learn a distribution from examples through a generator and a discriminator. Their training objective has a saddle point structure, with the two components pursuing opposing directions of optimization. The paper targets the training instability associated with that structure by changing the mathematical formulation of the discriminator’s part of the problem.

The authors begin with linear discriminators, where conjugate duality allows the saddle point objective to be rewritten as a maximization problem. In this formulation, the generator and the transformed discriminator work toward the same optimization direction. This is the central idea behind the proposed dualing GAN: reorganize the interaction that produces the training difficulty.

For GANs with linear discriminators, the approach is reported to remove training instability. The paper also extends the underlying intuition to nonlinear formulations, producing an alternative to the usual training algorithm. The distinction matters: the abstract makes the stronger stability claim for the linear case, while presenting the nonlinear extension as another training approach without asserting the same guarantee.
neurips-2017-dualing-gans-2782af9e38.tldr: Dualizing the discriminator removes reported training instability for linear-discriminator GANs and motivates an alternative training method for nonlinear GANs.

paragraphs: Supervised datasets often combine observations from several conditions, such as recordings from different people. A condition identifier tells the model which observations belong together, but does not directly describe the hidden properties that distinguish conditions. This paper asks how to learn those properties jointly and use them to handle a new condition with only a few observations.

The proposed Latent Variable Multiple Output Gaussian Process model combines regression across conditions with a learned latent space. It infers uncertainty over the Gaussian processes together with representations of the conditions. This lets the model capture information about their differences as part of the regression problem, rather than treating the identifiers alone as a complete description.

The authors derive a variational inference method whose computational complexity is as low as that of sparse Gaussian processes. They report significant improvements over related Gaussian process methods on tasks involving synthetic and real data. The contribution combines adaptation to sparsely observed new conditions with an inference procedure designed to keep the joint latent modeling computationally practical.
neurips-2017-efficient-modeling-of-laten.tldr: A Gaussian process model learns latent relationships among conditions to support regression and adaptation to new conditions from few observations.

paragraphs: A covariance matrix describes how variables fluctuate together. Estimating it becomes more challenging when the data have heavy tails, so unusually large observations occur more readily than in well-behaved sub-Gaussian settings. The paper addresses this gap by proposing a covariance estimator with theoretical guarantees that require only weak distributional assumptions, including the existence of low-order moments.

The main analysis establishes tight deviation inequalities for the estimator. These inequalities control how far its estimate can depart from the population covariance. Their dependence is expressed through parameters describing the covariance matrix’s intrinsic dimension, rather than the full number of coordinates in each observation.

That distinction matters for high-dimensional data: the number of recorded variables need not be the only measure governing the guarantee. The covariance structure itself determines the relevant intrinsic-dimension parameters. The result provides a theoretically supported strategy for heavy-tailed covariance estimation and applies to high-dimensional observations, extending the available analysis beyond the better-understood sub-Gaussian case.
neurips-2017-estimation-of-the-covarianc.tldr: A covariance estimator obtains tight error guarantees for heavy-tailed data using intrinsic-dimension parameters and weak moment assumptions.

paragraphs: Exponential-family distributions support efficient calculations through their natural parameters. The t-exponential family broadens this framework to include Student-t distributions, which are useful for handling noisy data. However, its deformed exponential changes the algebra, so an expectation propagation algorithm cannot simply be derived in the same way as for the ordinary exponential family.

The paper uses q-algebra from statistical physics to address this obstacle. It shows how a property called pseudo additivity enables calculations on t-exponential distributions through natural parameters. This supplies the mathematical machinery needed to recover a convenient computational representation despite the change in the underlying family.

Using that machinery, the authors develop an expectation propagation procedure that deterministically approximates posterior or predictive distributions through simple moment matching. They apply it to the Bayes point machine and Student-t process classification and demonstrate performance numerically. The contribution links a richer distribution family with a workable inference algorithm, making its noise-handling motivation compatible with structured approximate Bayesian computation.
neurips-2017-expectation-propagation-for.tldr: Using q-algebra, the paper develops moment-matching expectation propagation for the t-exponential family, including Student-t distributions.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why deep networks can perform well beyond their training examples. It examines several proposed explanations: controlling parameter norms, measuring sharpness, and studying robustness. The aim is to understand both how these quantities can support generalization guarantees and how well they account for behavior observed in deep learning.

A central point is the importance of scale normalization. When a proposed measure is used to explain generalization, the scale on which it is evaluated affects how it should be interpreted. The paper highlights this issue while studying the candidate measures, making normalization part of the analysis rather than treating the measures as immediately comparable quantities.

The authors also connect sharpness with PAC-Bayes theory, placing this proposed explanation in a framework for reasoning about generalization. They then investigate whether the measures explain different observed phenomena. The contribution is an examination of the relationship between theoretical guarantees and explanatory usefulness: a measure’s ability to support a bound and its ability to explain observed behavior are both subjects of the study.
neurips-2017-exploring-generalization-in.tldr: The paper examines norm, sharpness, and robustness explanations of deep-network generalization, emphasizing scale normalization and a connection to PAC-Bayes theory.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning often represents an optimal value function with a compact neural network representation. This can become difficult when the value function does not fit naturally into a low-dimensional description, making learning slow or unstable. Hybrid Reward Architecture addresses this problem by changing how the learning task is divided.

The method takes a reward function that has already been decomposed into components and learns a separate value function for each one. A component typically depends on only some of the available features. Its value function can therefore be easier to approximate with a compact representation, allowing learning to focus on simpler pieces of the overall reward.

The authors demonstrate the architecture on a toy problem and on Ms. Pac-Man, where it achieves above-human performance. The result supports reward decomposition as a useful way to approach domains with difficult value functions. The method’s premise is consequential: it receives a decomposed reward function, and the simplification depends on the component rewards typically involving smaller subsets of features.
neurips-2017-hybrid-reward-architecture-.tldr: Hybrid Reward Architecture learns separate value functions for decomposed rewards and achieves above-human performance on Ms. Pac-Man.

paragraphs: A Gaussian process state space model describes a changing system whose hidden states evolve through unknown, potentially nonlinear relationships. Gaussian processes represent the unknown transition or measurement mappings. This paper focuses on learning those mappings from observations, addressing system identification rather than only estimating hidden states after the model has already been specified.

The authors approximate the posterior over latent states with a structured Gaussian distribution parameterized by a bidirectional recurrent neural network. Processing a sequence in both directions supports a smoothed posterior over its hidden states. The structure therefore brings information across the observed sequence into the inference procedure used to learn the system.

A practical algorithm uses the reparameterization trick to compute a lower bound on the marginal likelihood efficiently. The construction also permits arbitrary kernels within the model, broadening the relationships its Gaussian processes can express. The authors demonstrate that learned models can efficiently generate plausible future trajectories after observing only a small number of episodes from the true system.
neurips-2017-identification-of-gaussian-.tldr: Structured variational inference with a bidirectional recurrent network enables efficient learning of Gaussian process state space models from few observed episodes.

paragraphs: A convolutional classifier is usually trained to distinguish examples, but this paper gives the classifier a generative role as well. The proposed introspective convolutional network can synthesize new samples within its own discriminative model. The authors use that capability as part of training, linking sample generation directly to improving classification.

Training follows an iterative reclassification-by-synthesis procedure derived from a Bayesian formulation. The network first generates pseudo-negative examples and then improves its classification using the resulting training process. Repeating these steps lets synthesis and discrimination contribute to the development of the same model. The final learned CNN retains both classification and sample-generation capabilities.

The authors evaluate the approach on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN using state-of-the-art CNN architectures and observe improved classification results. The findings support the value of adding this generative training mechanism to a classifier in the tested settings. The central contribution is the integration: the model’s own ability to produce examples becomes a resource for learning to distinguish them.
neurips-2017-introspective-classificatio.tldr: Introspective convolutional networks alternate between synthesizing pseudo-negative samples and improving classification, with reported gains on three image benchmarks.

paragraphs: The k-support and ordered weighted l1 norms extend ordinary l1 regularization to better handle correlated variables and improve prediction. This paper studies what happens when these penalties are extended to variables organized into overlapping groups. Such overlap makes the computational problem substantially harder: the resulting norms are generally NP-hard to compute.

The authors identify tractable cases through the structure of the groups. They develop a dynamic program for projecting a vector onto vectors supported by a fixed number of groups. The algorithm uses tree decompositions, and its complexity depends on treewidth, making the arrangement of overlaps central to whether the computation is manageable.

The dynamic program can also be transformed into an extended formulation for the corresponding k-group support norms and an overlapping-group version of the ordered weighted l1 norm. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of these new penalties. The contribution combines a hardness result with constructive algorithms, showing that useful overlapping-group regularization remains computationally accessible for certain group collections.
neurips-2017-k-support-and-ordered-weigh.tldr: Overlapping-group extensions of k-support and ordered weighted penalties are generally hard to compute, but structured group collections admit treewidth-dependent algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies online prediction for discrete-time linear dynamical systems with a symmetric transition matrix. Directly learning a system in its original form leads to a nonconvex optimization problem. The authors instead construct a larger prediction class that makes the learning objective convex, trading a controlled increase in representation size for easier optimization.

This approach uses improper learning: the predictor need not itself belong to the original class of linear dynamical systems. The enlargement is only by a polylogarithmic factor. Its core operation is spectral filtering, which convolves the time series with eigenvectors of a particular Hankel matrix to produce the representation used for prediction.

The resulting algorithm runs in polynomial time and has a near-optimal regret guarantee for online prediction. The paper also derives a corresponding sample complexity bound for agnostic learning. Together, these results show how a carefully chosen expanded representation can bypass nonconvex fitting while retaining strong prediction guarantees for the stated class of systems.
neurips-2017-learning-linear-dynamical-s.tldr: Spectral filtering enables convex, polynomial-time online prediction with near-optimal regret for linear dynamical systems with symmetric transitions.

paragraphs: Long-tailed datasets contain a few well-represented classes and many classes with little training data. This paper treats learning the rare classes as a transfer problem: use the data-rich classes to learn how a model changes when more examples become available, then apply that knowledge to models trained on scarce data.

The method trains a meta-network in the space of model parameters. Its input is a model learned from few examples, and its target is the parameters of a model learned from many examples. Transfer proceeds gradually from the head of the class distribution through its body to its tail. Meta-networks trained with more data regularize those handling fewer examples.

This progressive construction captures a notion of model dynamics, predicting how parameters are likely to evolve as training data increase. On SUN, Places, and ImageNet datasets adjusted for long-tailed classification, the approach significantly outperforms common resampling and reweighting heuristics. The stated results support transferring knowledge about the learning process itself to improve data-poor classes.
neurips-2017-learning-to-model-the-tail-.tldr: Progressive meta-networks transfer how model parameters change with more data from common classes to rare classes, improving long-tailed image classification.

paragraphs: Undirected graphical models express relationships among variables without assigning a direction to each connection. Learning them involves the partition function, which normalizes the model’s probabilities. This paper proposes black-box learning and inference algorithms that work by optimizing a variational approximation to the model’s log-likelihood, bringing this normalization quantity into the approximation.

The central construction is an upper bound on the log-partition function. A function q parameterizes the bound, and the authors represent q with a flexible neural network. This makes the bound part of a trainable framework and allows the partition function to be tracked while the model itself is being learned.

The framework also enables faster sampling and unified variational training for a broad class of models that combine directed and undirected components. Experiments on several generative modeling datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution is thus broader than a single model architecture: the neural parameterization supports a shared approach to normalization, inference, and learning across the stated model classes.
neurips-2017-neural-variational-inferenc.tldr: A neural variational bound on the log-partition function supports learning, inference, and faster sampling in undirected and hybrid graphical models.

paragraphs: In the pooled data problem, each test examines a group of items and reports how many items carry each label. The task is to reconstruct the individual labels from these aggregate counts. This paper asks how many pooled tests are fundamentally required, distinguishing the information contained in the observations from the mechanics of a particular decoding algorithm.

For noiseless observations and optimal decoding, the authors identify an exact asymptotic threshold in the number of tests. They prove a phase transition separating complete recovery from complete failure. This describes a sharp change in what is recoverable as the available number of tests crosses the threshold in the asymptotic setting.

The paper also introduces a noisy version and develops an information-theoretic framework for general random noise models. Its results show that even low noise can strictly worsen the scaling of the required test count. Similar behavior appears when some labeling mistakes are permitted, showing that allowing approximate recovery does not eliminate the demonstrated sensitivity to noise.
neurips-2017-phase-transitions-in-the-po.tldr: The paper identifies a sharp noiseless recovery threshold for pooled labels and shows that even low noise can worsen required test-count scaling.

paragraphs: Dual volume sampling selects columns from a short, wide matrix using probabilities determined by the volume spanned by the selected submatrix’s rows. For an n-by-m matrix, it selects k columns with n ≤ k ≤ m. The method is useful for column subset selection, but the absence of polynomial-time sampling algorithms had limited its practical adoption.

The paper develops an exact randomized polynomial-time sampling algorithm and a derandomization. This resolves the stated computational obstacle to carrying out dual volume sampling. The authors then analyze the sampling distribution using real stable polynomials and establish that it has the Strong Rayleigh property.

That structural result yields further consequences, including a Markov chain sampler with a provably fast mixing rate. It supplies another computational route to the distribution, backed by an analysis of convergence. The sampler is also closely related to classical experimental-design algorithms that work well empirically but lack theoretical analysis, connecting the new guarantees with established practical methods.
neurips-2017-polynomial-time-algorithms-.tldr: Exact polynomial-time algorithms and a Strong Rayleigh analysis make dual volume sampling computationally accessible and yield a fast-mixing sampler.

paragraphs: Robust optimization seeks a solution that performs well against the worst objective in a specified collection. For nonconvex problems, finding such a solution can be difficult. This paper connects the robust problem to stochastic optimization, where an optimization procedure instead handles a distribution over objectives.

The reduction assumes access to an oracle that returns α-approximate solutions for distributions over objectives. Using that oracle, the method constructs a distribution over solutions with an α-approximation guarantee in the worst case. The form of the output matters: the robust guarantee is obtained for a randomized choice among solutions, which is why the paper describes the optimization as improper.

Turning that distribution into a deterministic solution is NP-hard in general, although the authors show it can be done for a broad class of statistical learning tasks. They apply the framework to robust neural network training and submodular optimization, with experiments on corrupted character classification and robust influence maximization. The contribution separates the attainable randomized guarantee from the additional difficulty of derandomization.
neurips-2017-robust-optimization-for-non.tldr: A reduction turns approximate stochastic optimization into worst-case robust optimization over distributions of solutions, while characterizing the difficulty of derandomization.

paragraphs: Importance sampling can accelerate optimization by choosing updates according to their importance instead of uniformly. Ideally, the sampling probabilities would adapt to the changing gradients. Computing all the gradient information needed for that choice can be too expensive, however, undermining the benefit of the adaptive procedure.

The paper proposes an approximation based on safe bounds on the gradients. These bounds support a sampling distribution that is provably best relative to the available bounds. The authors also establish superiority over uniform sampling and fixed importance sampling in their sampling analysis. This provides a principled way to adapt the distribution without requiring complete current gradient information.

The distribution can be computed efficiently, with negligible additional cost in many applications. The scheme is generic enough to fit existing optimization algorithms, and the paper shows that coordinate descent and stochastic gradient descent can gain significant speedups. Extensive numerical testing supports the efficiency analysis. The practical attraction is the combination of adaptive update selection with a cost low enough to preserve its computational benefit.
neurips-2017-safe-adaptive-importance-sa.tldr: Safe gradient bounds enable efficient adaptive sampling with theoretical sampling advantages and demonstrated optimization speedups.

paragraphs: Optical flow estimates motion between video frames. Training convolutional networks for this task requires many examples with known motion, so supervised approaches often use synthetic data. Real videos provide plentiful unlabeled observations, but unsupervised methods commonly depend on brightness constancy and spatial smoothness assumptions that break down near motion boundaries.

The paper proposes semi-supervised optical flow learning with a generative adversarial network, allowing unlabeled videos to contribute to training. Its key idea is to use an adversarial loss to capture structural patterns in flow warp errors. This gives the learning procedure a way to evaluate those patterns without explicitly imposing the assumptions identified as problematic.

Extensive benchmark experiments show favorable performance against purely supervised and other semi-supervised schemes. The findings support learning from the structure of warp errors as a useful complement to available supervision. The approach matters because it connects unlabeled real-world video to optical flow training while addressing a specific weakness of objectives built around fixed brightness and smoothness assumptions.
neurips-2017-semi-supervised-learning-fo.tldr: An adversarial loss learns structural patterns in flow warp errors, enabling semi-supervised optical flow training with unlabeled videos.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks often transfer successfully from images to other spatial data, but spherical geometry introduces complications that ordinary image architectures do not automatically resolve. This paper develops ways to perform convolution on the sphere, aiming to make neural feature learning work with data whose natural organization is spherical.

The authors introduce two grid strategies: spherical-polar coordinates and a cubed-sphere representation. They examine the challenges of convolution in these settings and extend the discussion to spherical volumes. For volumes, they also consider several ways to parameterize radial distance, addressing how information varies both around a sphere and outward from its center.

As a proof of concept, the paper studies structural environments within proteins. The models learn nontrivial functions and generally outperform standard three-dimensional convolutions in that setting. Without domain-specific feature engineering, they also achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods built on substantial domain knowledge. These results support the usefulness of matching the convolutional representation to molecular spatial structure in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2017-spherical-convolutions-and-.tldr: Two spherical convolution strategies learn useful protein-environment functions and generally outperform standard 3D convolutions in the evaluated setting.

paragraphs: Stein variational gradient descent approximates a target distribution by deterministically moving a collection of particles. Its update is chosen to decrease KL divergence optimally within a function space. This paper develops a theoretical account of that particle transport, connecting the algorithm’s updates with the evolution of probability distributions.

The authors establish weak convergence of the empirical distributions represented by the particles to the target distribution. They also characterize SVGD’s asymptotic behavior through a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation known as the Vlasov equation. This connects the discrete collection of moving particles with a continuous description of how their distribution changes.

A geometric interpretation ties these results together: SVGD is a gradient flow of KL divergence under a new metric on the space of distributions, induced by the Stein operator. The contribution gives a mathematical interpretation of the algorithm’s direction of movement and its limiting behavior. It explains particle-based approximation through distributional geometry, with convergence expressed in the weak sense established by the analysis.
neurips-2017-stein-variational-gradient-.tldr: The paper analyzes SVGD convergence and interprets its particle dynamics as a KL-divergence gradient flow under a Stein-induced metric.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning guarantees can describe performance through probably approximately correct learning or through regret. These frameworks capture different aspects of how an algorithm learns, leaving a gap between their guarantees. This paper introduces Uniform-PAC, a stronger version of the classical PAC framework, to connect the two forms of analysis.

The key property is that Uniform-PAC guarantees can be used to derive high-probability regret guarantees, something the classical PAC framework does not provide in the same way. The framework therefore offers a shared theoretical basis for reasoning about approximate correctness and the performance cost accumulated while learning.

The authors demonstrate the framework for finite-state episodic Markov decision processes with a new algorithm. It is Uniform-PAC and simultaneously achieves regret and PAC guarantees that are optimal except for a factor depending on the horizon. The result makes the connection constructive: one algorithm supports both types of assurance, with the remaining horizon factor explicitly qualifying the optimality claim. This is relevant to settings where formal learning guarantees matter.
neurips-2017-unifying-pac-and-regret-uni.tldr: Uniform-PAC links PAC and high-probability regret guarantees, with an episodic RL algorithm achieving both optimally up to a horizon factor.

paragraphs: Counterfactual approaches to fair prediction depend on a causal explanation of how the data were generated. Yet the available observations generally cannot validate every causal implication without further assumptions. This paper addresses the resulting uncertainty by considering several competing causal models when learning a fair classifier.

The authors formulate prediction as an optimization problem with fairness constraints supplied by the competing causal explanations. They show that predictions can be approximately fair with respect to multiple models at once, and that the optimization can be solved efficiently with gradient-based methods. This reduces dependence on committing to one exact causal specification.

Experiments on two real-world fair classification problems demonstrate the framework’s flexibility and its ability to balance prediction accuracy with fairness across the considered worlds. The qualification is central: the result concerns approximate fairness relative to multiple supplied causal models. Its value is to bring disagreement about causal assumptions into the learning objective itself, allowing that uncertainty to influence the fairness–accuracy balance.
neurips-2017-when-worlds-collide-integra.tldr: Fairness constraints from competing causal models enable predictions that balance accuracy with approximate counterfactual fairness across multiple possible worlds.
